summary: Suggests adding language abstractions to YANG, the data modeling language used with NETCONF, to improve extensibility and reuse of models. This is an experimental specification and the proposed features were meant to be tried out rather than adopted as is.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to add handy building blocks to a language used for describing network settings, so people can reuse parts instead of rewriting them. It was a trial idea.

subtitle: Language features to improve reuse and structure in YANG data models.

tldr.problem: YANG data models often need to represent inheritance, recursive structures, and type-safe references, but the original YANG language lacked language abstractions like class inheritance and typed identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes complex types (which can extend other types and include recursive structures), typed instance identifiers, and abstract types as extensions to YANG's syntax and semantics.
tldr.outcome: The extensions were published as experimental to be tried out by implementers. They allow models to better match object-oriented designs and reduce redundancy, though adoption remained limited as YANG evolved separately.

facts.label: Main features
facts.value: Complex types, inheritance, typed references, recursion

today: RFC 6095 remains an experimental specification. While complex types were never integrated into the official YANG standard, the concepts influenced later YANG developments. The RFC demonstrates both the strengths of experimental documents in exploring new design directions and the reality that not all experimental proposals achieve standards-track status.

sections.title: Why YANG Needs Language Abstractions
sections.content:
YANG is the data modeling language for NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol). It lets engineers describe the configuration and status information of network devices as a tree of data elements.

Real-world network management systems often use object-oriented design—they organize managed resources as classes that inherit from base classes, define abstract concepts, and reference each other in type-safe ways. When YANG models need to represent such designs, they face challenges: defining the same properties multiple times for similar resources, representing recursive containment hierarchies (like a chassis containing slots containing cards), and creating associations between objects without knowing their exact location in the tree.

This RFC proposes extending YANG with language features to address these challenges: complex types (for class-like definitions and inheritance), typed instance identifiers (for type-safe references), and abstract types (for base concepts that must be refined before use).
sections.plainLanguage: When network people design systems, they think about classes and inheritance, like how all equipment is hardware, but a card is a special kind of equipment. YANG couldn't express this directly, so people had to write the same information over and over.

sections.title: Complex Types and Inheritance
sections.content:
Complex types: A complex type is a named template for a structured data element with rich internal content. It can contain leaves (simple values), lists, containers, choices, and other YANG constructs, similar to a grouping but with additional semantics.

Inheritance via extends: A complex type can extend an existing complex type using the ct:extends statement, creating a specialized version. For example, a PhysicalConnector type can extend the Hardware type, inheriting all its properties while adding new ones specific to connectors. An instance of the derived type can be used anywhere an instance of the base type is expected.

Abstract types: A complex type can be declared abstract using the ct:abstract statement. Abstract types serve as base classes and cannot be instantiated directly—only their concrete subclasses can appear in NETCONF payloads. This enforces that specialization is required before creation.

Instance and instance-list: The ct:instance and ct:instance-list statements create individual or multiple instantiations of a complex type within the data tree. They are similar to YANG's leaf and leaf-list but define a structured subtree according to the type's definition.
sections.plainLanguage: Complex types are like blueprints. You can create a blueprint for 'Hardware', then create more specific blueprints for 'Equipment' and 'Connector' that build on 'Hardware' and add new details. When you use these blueprints in a model, you're creating instances of the type.

sections.title: Typed Instance Identifiers
sections.content:
YANG's existing instance-identifier type allows referencing any node in the data tree, but offers no type safety. The proposed instance-identifier with instance-type restricts references to instances of a specific complex type (or its subtypes).

For example, in a model of physical equipment where different parts connect to each other, instead of generic leafref nodes that could point anywhere, you can define typed references that say 'this leaf must reference a PhysicalConnector instance'. This prevents errors at the model level and makes the intent clear.

The type information is encoded in the NETCONF payload using special XML elements (cti:type), allowing parsers to determine the actual type of each instance without needing separate metadata fields.
sections.plainLanguage: With typed references, you can say 'this connection must link to a Card-type device, not just any device'. The system checks this is true, preventing mistakes where you try to connect incompatible pieces.

sections.title: Recursive Structures
sections.content:
Many management systems model containment hierarchies recursively. For example, a chassis contains equipment holders, which contain equipment, which may contain further equipment holders. In pure YANG, representing this required flat lists with cross-references.

Complex types enable true recursive containment: a complex type can directly contain instances of itself or its ancestor types. An EquipmentHolder complex type can contain equipment instances of type Equipment, which may in turn contain nested equipment elements. This allows the data tree to reflect the actual containment hierarchy.

Recursive structures are useful for representing arbitrary-depth hierarchies like file systems, organizational structures, and network topologies where the structure itself is the primary organizing principle.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine Russian nesting dolls where each doll can contain smaller dolls of the same kind. Recursive structures let you model things that nest inside themselves to any depth, like boxes inside boxes.

sections.title: Design and Benefits
sections.content:
These extensions were designed to reuse existing YANG statements and semantics wherever possible, minimizing disruption to existing YANG knowledge. New functionality is added via extension statements like ct:complex-type, ct:extends, and ct:instance.

Modeling benefits include:

  • Nearly one-to-one mapping between object-oriented class hierarchies and YANG complex types
  • Elimination of metadata fields that track type information—the actual type is part of the payload
  • Natural representation of containment hierarchies without flattening
  • Concept refinement through type extension rather than workarounds like large choice statements
  • Reuse of properties across related resource types through inheritance
  • Avoidance of duplication when modeling variants of a concept

The RFC was published experimentally, with implementations in tools like Pyang and Libsmi to encourage testing and feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: These features make YANG models cleaner and easier to write because they let you define a base type once, then specialize it, rather than repeating the whole definition each time. Code in other languages already works this way.
